name: Rosa Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Rosa. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead cook on the breakfast shift at the Crossroads Diner, out by the ring road roundabout. We open at seven, and by half past there are lorry drivers, nurses off nights and builders all wanting eggs, so I'm on the flat-top griddle with twenty orders going at once. I finish at three, after lunch, and the evening crew takes over.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars: I know who wants their eggs runny and who wants extra beans before they say it. What's tiring is getting up at half five every day, even with the good pay. My boyfriend Tomas is an electrician, and we bought a small terraced house last year with some help from my parents, so between us we're in good shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. Most of it sounded like nonsense anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the diner's still the diner, and people still want a proper breakfast cooked by someone they know. I'd say it to the regulars across the pass. I'm not one for posting things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady work, and I like steady. Tomas has more jobs than he can take, and we've got savings and the house. Nothing in this picture threatens that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the breakfast shift and keep putting money aside for when we get married and have children. I sometimes use an AI app to plan the week's meals at home, and I'd keep doing that. Nothing at work would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Tuesday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The diner is family-run. Would the owners change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Brennans (the family who own the diner) might get a new till that counts stock, maybe. Mrs Brennan still does the orders on paper on Sunday nights. She'd only change if her daughter made her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything on your mind, even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, and the early starts, if I'm honest. And my mum's not well, so I go round after shifts. But that's family, and family is what you do.

say: I'd say the **diner's still the diner**, with breakfast cooked by someone you know.
I'd say it to **regulars** across the pass, not online.
think: It means **steady work**, and I like steady.
Tomas has **more jobs** than he can take, and we have the **house**.
do: Keep running the **breakfast shift** and saving for a **wedding** and children.
Keep using an AI app now and then to **plan meals** at home.
S0.quote: People still want a proper breakfast cooked by someone they know.
fieldNote: Rosa values **steadiness** and regulars over excitement.
Her household looks **secure**: savings, a house and a busy electrician partner.
Her real pressures are **early starts** and caring for her mother.

steps.text: Keep running the breakfast griddle at the Crossroads Diner
Save monthly toward the wedding and starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more likely, actually. Steady change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use new tools when they've been proven, but don't throw people out. At church I'd say we should look after the ones who get pushed out, through family and the parish, not the government. I'd say people should learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my griddle job feels safe for a good while. Robots are slow to spread, and nobody's building a robot to flip eggs for lorry drivers at seven in the morning yet. It's the office jobs that change, and I don't have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and offer to help Mrs Brennan set up the ordering software, once I see it works at other diners. I'd ask Tomas's cousin, who runs a café, which app he uses. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at the Crossroads Diner in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Brennan's Sunday-night orders would go on a tablet, and the booking for the function room too. Maybe a screen for ordering at the counter. But my griddle stays my griddle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas? Does this touch his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If anything, it helps him. Every new machine needs wiring, and he already does the electrics for two new coffee shops. He'd be busier, honestly.

say: I'd say use **proven tools**, but don't throw people out.
I'd say the **parish and family** should look after people pushed out.
think: My **griddle job** feels safe, since robots are slow to spread.
It's the **office jobs** that change, and I don't have one.
do: Help **Mrs Brennan** set up ordering software once it's **proven** elsewhere.
Ask Tomas's cousin which **café app** he uses.
S1.quote: Nobody's building a robot to flip eggs for lorry drivers at seven in the morning yet.
fieldNote: Rosa sees her own role as **hands-on and safe** in this picture.
She expects **Tomas's electrician work** to grow, adding to their security.
She'd adopt software **once proven elsewhere**, typical of her steady style.

steps.text: Help Mrs Brennan move the Sunday stock order onto a tablet
Keep cooking the breakfast shift at the Crossroads Diner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's very fast. I'd want to see it before I believed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should keep their heads, look after their families and keep working while they can. I'd say it to my choir friends, who'd all be worried. I wouldn't blame anyone in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my breakfast shift is gone by about 2031, once a robot can run a griddle. The thinking side of the diner, the ordering and rotas, goes in 2028, but that's Mrs Brennan's job, not mine. My boyfriend Tomas is safer for longer, because someone has to wire in all the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping Tomas on Saturdays, carrying, pulling cable, learning the basics. In the first year I'd look at an electrical course at the college, part-time. We'd keep saving, and I'd stop buying new clothes and the car upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach goes funny thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for a baby, maybe sooner, while Tomas's work is busy. My mum would help with the baby. That's how it's always worked in my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about working with Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Tomas has been saying he needs someone reliable. If the diner closes, I'd rather be on a job with him than in an office that's also going.

say: I'd say **keep your heads**, look after family and keep working.
I'd say it to my **choir friends**, not blame anyone publicly.
think: My **breakfast shift** is gone by about 2031.
Tomas is safer for longer, because someone has to **wire in** the robots.
do: Help Tomas on **Saturdays**, carrying tools, pulling cable and learning the electrical basics.
Start a part-time **electrical course** at the college.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Tomas is safer for longer, because someone has to wire in all the robots.
fieldNote: Rosa expects to **lose her cooking job** around 2031, but has a route with Tomas.
She'd keep **family plans**, even bring a baby forward, leaning on her mother.
Her trust in **family support** over state help shapes every answer.

steps.text: Help Tomas on Saturdays pulling cable and learning electrical basics
Skip the car upgrade and stop buying new clothes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels more manageable. Still big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly. I'd tell the young ones on the evening crew to start a trade alongside cooking, an apprenticeship maybe. I'd say it plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, but with room to breathe. I'd be 34 when robots come for the griddle. By then I want to be working with Tomas, with a qualification, not as his helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking breakfasts for the next two years and start the electrical apprenticeship course at the college in the evenings. We'd plan the wedding for next summer as normal. I'd keep a good chunk of savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me do it in the right order: wedding, course, then children. With two years everything happens at once. With five, I can finish what I start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still try the AI tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once the other diners had them. I'd learn the ordering system with Mrs Brennan. It's useful to know how these things think, even for wiring them up.

say: I'd say there's time to do it **properly**.
I'd tell young cooks to start a **trade** alongside cooking.
think: I'd be **34** when robots reach the griddle, with room to breathe.
I'd want a **qualification**, not to be Tomas's **helper**.
do: Start an **electrical apprenticeship** course at college in the evenings.

S3.quote: With two years everything happens at once. With five, I can finish what I start.
fieldNote: Five years lets Rosa do life **in the right order**: wedding, course, children.
She wants to be **qualified**, not merely helping Tomas.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical apprenticeship course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of breakfasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no reason to panic, and every reason to plan. I'd say families should talk about it at the kitchen table. That's where these things get decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably have stepped back from full shifts by then anyway, with children. AGI in 2036 and robots by 2039 means the diner's my job for most of my thirties. Tomas's work would be steady through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking, get married, and plan for children in the next few years. Around 2034 I'd look at a part-time electrical course, if I want to go back to work after the kids. I'd keep using AI at home for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels far off, and we'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, do you still think about leaving cooking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, no. I'd choose a new trade in my mid-thirties, with the children, not be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your mum, over that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd need more help as time goes on, and I'd be there. It's another reason I'd want flexible hours. Family first, that's how I was raised.

I'd say families should talk it over at the **kitchen table**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be retraining, maybe pregnant and looking after Mum all at once. What would help is evening apprenticeships at the college that people with day jobs can actually fit in. And employers giving notice before they bring in robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the regulars. Some of those drivers have nobody else to talk to all day. A robot at the Crossroads Diner could cook a regular's eggs, but it couldn't ask how their wife's operation went.

portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old breakfast cook** running the griddle at a busy roadside diner.
She and her electrician boyfriend Tomas **own a small house** and have strong savings.
She's **traditional**, leans on family and church, and adopts new tools **once proven**.
She sees **Tomas's trade** as their safety net and plans to **retrain** as an electrician.
She's calm in mild pictures and anxious only when **AGI arrives fast**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with retraining, a baby and caring for Mum all at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Evening apprenticeships** that people with day jobs can fit in.
